units.title: Square-integrable mixed Brownian increment sums
units.statement: For two distinct coordinates of one Euclidean Brownian motion, the predictably weighted dyadic mixed increment sum is in L² at each level and converges to zero in mean square.
assumptions: One Euclidean Brownian driver and its given filtration.
Distinct coordinates and square-integrable weights measurable at each left endpoint.
One uniform second-moment bound on the weights. T may be zero.
units.formula: C_n=\sum_i w_{n,i}\Delta_i B^j\,\Delta_i B^k,\qquad C_n\in L^2,\qquad \mathbb E[C_n^2]\longrightarrow0.

proof.title: Build a third unit projection
proof.text: Use the normalized sum of the two orthogonal coordinate vectors.

proof.title: Polarize the increments
proof.text: The compensated time terms cancel, leaving the product of the two actual coordinate increments.

proof.title: Transfer the scalar limits
proof.text: The three compensated sums are square integrable. The mixed squared expectation is bounded by a fixed linear combination of their squared expectations.

units.boundary: The actual mixed sum is square integrable on each deterministic grid.

units.title: The projected Hessian trace removes the radial term
units.statement: Let $w$ be a unit vector in a real Euclidean space with finite coordinate set $I$, let $(e_j)_{j\in I}$ be its coordinate basis, and let $f$ be a real ambient test function. Write $p_j=e_j-w_jw$. The trace of the ambient second Fréchet derivative evaluated on the pairs $(p_j,p_j)$ equals the ambient Laplacian minus the radial Hessian entry.
assumptions: The finite coordinate set has decidable equality. The point $w$ has Euclidean norm one.

For an analytic interpretation of the Hessian, take a twice continuously differentiable ambient test near $w$. The Lean equality itself is algebraic in the totalized Fréchet derivatives and has no smoothness premise.

proof.title: Expand the projected arguments
proof.text: Bilinearity gives two mixed radial terms and one term with two radial arguments for each coordinate.
proof.formula: D^2 f[p_j,p_j]=D^2 f[e_j,e_j]-w_jD^2 f[e_j,w]-w_jD^2 f[w,e_j]+w_j^2D^2 f[w,w].

proof.title: Sum the radial contributions
proof.text: The coordinate expansion of $w$ makes each mixed sum equal to the radial Hessian entry. The unit norm makes the squared-coordinate sum one. The remaining diagonal sum is Mathlib's ambient Laplacian.

units.boundary: The equation is pointwise at a unit vector. It concerns the extrinsic trace in ambient coordinates.

units.title: The actual vector Itô Taylor residual vanishes
units.statement: For the completed Euclidean Itô process staying in a compact K throughout the horizon almost surely, and a scalar test twice continuously Fréchet differentiable at every point of K, the sum of second-order Taylor residuals along its dyadic increments converges in measure to zero.
assumptions: The positive horizon is T. The sample measure is finite, the filtration satisfies the usual conditions, and the driving standard vector Brownian motion is relative to that filtration and measure.
The finite coordinate rows have progressive product-square-integrable diffusion coefficients. Their drift evaluations at each fixed time t≤T are almost-everywhere strongly measurable.
The drift paths are almost surely continuous and have bounded variation on [0,T].

The compact set K has a selected fallback point k₀. On one event of full measure, the process belongs to K at every time in [0,T]. The test is twice continuously Fréchet differentiable at each point of that range.

proof.title: Place the paths in the compact range
proof.text: Clip the time at T and apply the Borel fallback outside K. On the event where the original path stays in K, the resulting K-valued path agrees with it at every dyadic grid point.

proof.title: Derive the coordinate square-sum limits
proof.text: At the terminal grid point the inclusive prefix contains all fine cells. The scalar quadratic-variation theorem supplies the limit for each actual coordinate.

proof.title: Apply the Taylor residual estimate
proof.text: Apply the existing Euclidean residual theorem using these coordinate limits. Equality of the clipped and original paths on the grids gives the claimed sum.

units.boundary: The conclusion is convergence in measure on the specified positive horizon. The dyadic residuals are evaluated on the original process.

units.title: The linear Itô term and its completed martingale
units.statement: Take the almost surely compact-range Euclidean process built from initialized drift time primitives and completed stochastic integrals. For a continuously Fréchet differentiable test on that range, the left-endpoint derivative sums converge in measure to the integral of the derivative applied to the drift vector plus the terminal value of a genuine martingale.
assumptions: The horizon T is positive and the sample measure is finite. The filtration satisfies the usual conditions and the standard vector Brownian motion is relative to that filtration and measure.
The state and Brownian coordinate types are finite with decidable equality. Each diffusion entry is progressive and square-integrable in the product of sample and horizon time measures.
The compact set K has a selected fallback point k₀. On one event of full measure, the process belongs to K at every time in [0,T].
Each initial coordinate is strongly measurable at time zero. Each drift coordinate is strongly progressive and has almost surely integrable time sections on the horizon.
The scalar test is continuously Fréchet differentiable at each point of K.

notation.text: The initial value, moving time primitive and completed Itô integrals define the vector process.
Each gradient entry uses the time-clipped process. The sum of the completed integrals is a martingale starting at zero.

proof.title: Take the weighted stochastic limits
proof.text: For each coordinate use the progressive bounded derivative weight. Apply the weighted stochastic-sum theorem to each actual completed integral to obtain the progressive L² product integrand.

proof.title: Take the weighted drift limit
proof.text: On almost every path, the initialized drift increments are increments of the integrable time primitive. The continuous derivative weight therefore gives the ordinary weighted time-integral limit. Almost-sure convergence implies convergence in measure under the finite sample measure.

proof.title: Assemble the genuine martingale
proof.text: Each weighted diffusion entry is a progressive L² integrand. Its completed stochastic integral is a martingale. Add them over the finite coordinate pairs. The sum is zero at time zero for every sample.

proof.title: Recover the derivative on the actual vectors
proof.text: The finite limits sum in measure. Expand the derivative on the actual increment in its basis, and move the finite drift sum inside the time integral using bounded weights and integrable drift sections.

units.boundary: This convergence identifies the first-order Taylor term. The quadratic term and the residual enter the full identity separately.

units.title: A uniform Taylor residual estimate on a compact set
units.statement: For every ε>0, there is one radius δ>0 that controls the second-order residual for every starting point x in K and every increment with norm less than δ.
assumptions: Let E and F be real normed vector spaces. Derivatives are real Fréchet derivatives; D²f(x) is viewed as a continuous bilinear map.
E is locally compact, K⊆E is compact, and f is C² at every point of K. The set K may be empty.

proof.title: Choose a compact neighborhood inside the smooth locus
proof.text: The C² locus is open. Compactness of K and local compactness of E give a compact closed neighborhood of K contained in that locus.

proof.title: Use uniform continuity of the Hessian
proof.text: The Hessian is continuous on this compact neighborhood, so a single distance threshold bounds its oscillation by ε.

proof.title: Keep every short segment in the neighborhood
proof.text: Take δ=min(ρ,δ₀). Every x+tv with x∈K, ‖v‖<δ and t∈[0,1] remains in the chosen neighborhood and within δ₀ of x. Apply the preceding segment estimate.

units.boundary: The required C² hypothesis is ambient at each point of K, stronger than merely having derivatives relative to K. No global derivative bound is assumed.

units.title: The extrinsic sphere Laplacian expression
units.statement: For a finite coordinate set I, define the following ambient real-valued expression for every f:ℝᴵ→ℝ and w∈ℝᴵ. On the unit sphere and for a C² ambient test this is the usual extrinsic formula for the sphere Laplacian.
assumptions: I is finite with decidable equality, E is Euclidean space ℝᴵ, f:E→ℝ and w∈E. The subtraction |I|−1 is natural-number subtraction before conversion to ℝ.

proof.title: Remove radial second and first derivatives
proof.text: The definition subtracts the radial Hessian and the radial first-derivative correction from the ambient Laplacian.

units.boundary: The definition is total off the sphere and without a smoothness assumption. It is an ambient expression; this declaration does not independently identify an intrinsic Laplace–Beltrami operator.

units.title: Vanishing Taylor residuals on a dyadic time grid
units.statement: For a compact-state process on [0,T], the sums of second-order Taylor residuals over the dyadic grids converge in measure to zero whenever the sums of squared increments converge in measure to a real-valued Q.
assumptions: The sample space Ω carries a finite measure μ. E is a locally compact real normed space with its Borel measurable structure. K⊆E is compact.
f:E→ℝ is C² at every point of K. Each time evaluation of the K-valued process X is measurable. Its paths are continuous on the specified compact time domain for μ-almost every sample.
T>0, X is defined at all nonnegative times and has almost-sure continuous paths on [0,T]. The dyadic sums of squared increments converge in measure to Q:Ω→ℝ.

proof.title: Restrict time to the compact interval
proof.text: Every dyadic time lies in [0,T]. Restrict X to this interval, retaining measurable time slices and almost-sure path continuity.

proof.title: Verify the mesh hypothesis and apply the grid theorem
proof.text: Consecutive grid points are exactly T/2ⁿ apart, so their distances tend to zero. All hypotheses of the arbitrary-grid residual theorem now hold.

units.boundary: This theorem transfers an assumed square-increment limit to a Taylor-residual limit; it does not itself prove quadratic variation for a stochastic integral.
